messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,
I am attempting to analyse my data on Distance for the first time, however I am not sure whether I am using the correct approach.

Last winter I carried out a bird survey in a semi-natural and in a planted forest using point transect sampling and I collected data on four different species. None of these species however, reach the suggested number of observations for point transects (80-100).

Considering that my primary aim is to compare the density estimates of the two types of forest stand, I post-stratified using the stratum layer (plantation and semi-natural) and set the level of resolution of estimates to stratum (hopefully that is correct?).
Now, seeing that my data include different species, should I use species as covariate, or this is used only when we want to estimate density for each species?
I hope this makes sense!

Thanks in advance,
Eleonora

Eleonora

Several questions:
you say your interest is in comparison of density between habitats.  If you took habitat types into consideration when you designed your study, allocating sufficient points to each habitat type, then you shouldn't need to post-stratify.  I presume you identified the habitat type of each point at the stratum level, correct?  Then simple stratification will produce the stratum-specific density estimates.
as I read your message, it seems you are not interested in species-specific density estimates, is that correct?  If you wish to produce habitat-specific avian density estimates (combined across species), then you need not incorporate species in the detection function, as pooling robustness can accommodate heterogeneity in detectability across species.

Let me know how much of this I have misunderstood.

messages.subject: Is MCDS (observer effect) bad for DSM?
messages.subject_clean: Is MCDS (observer effect) bad for DSM?
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

We conducted an
aerial line transect survey with two observers (left/right side of the aircraft). A
hazard-rate detection function with observer as factor covariate was selected by
AIC as an appropriate detection function (both observers had high detection near
the line, but one observer detected fewer animals in the distance ‘bin’
furthest away from the track-line.

I would appreciate your input to better understand the
implications of having a detection function with observer as a covariate for
DSM modelling. Particularly whether (or why) this is a negative outcome
relative to the situation where both left and right observers had the same
detection function. I’ll try to answer some of this myself, but appreciate your
corrections and additions to the statements below.

One negative aspect is that observer change within
segments and therefore we cannot use a count model for DSM, or dsm.var.prop for
variance propagation.

But what about
estimates of density in the DSM? Are these prone to bias because we have ‘observer effect’
present in the detection function? Instead of observed counts, we now use a Horvitz-Thompson-like
estimate of abundance per segment in the DSM. This takes into account the
detection probability (p), which in our case is the average probability
of detection from both observers (?)

Thanks in advance for any comments.

Chris

Hello Cornelia and whomever else this may concern,

I'm working my way through converting the example of Model-based inference analysis from Buckland et al (2015) at https://examples.distancesampling.org/book-bobwhite/bobwhite.html#defining-the-likelihood-function by Cornelia Oedekoven for my line-transect data.

I have the algorithm up and running for my line-transect data running ok - and I tested it (accidentally) first on survey data with only presence data. The chain was moving ok and I got reasonably good estimates that were similar to those of basic distance with the ds() function. However, when I realized my mistake (i.e. not including the absence data), and added in the absence data, the chain no longer moves.

While the algorithm will run, the trace plots are flat and do not move at all from their initial values.

I'm thinking it's because I don't have enough presences (n_obs=216) compared to the zeros. With all transects and all observations, my total is n_tot=418 for one of the years (2016) that I'm sampling. The other year's (2007) split in data is more drastic (n_obs= 54, n_total=1440); and I could understand 2007 having "too many zeros" but I'm confused why 2016 wouldn't work either. Is there something in the R code that I should adjust to allow for more zeros or should the algorithm be able to handle this, and there may be a mistake somewhere else?

messages.body_plain:
Chris, if both observers are operating simultaneously, one either side, then there is no problem.  As Eric notes, pooling robustness means all is OK.  If you had segments where one observer only is used, then segments where the other observer only operated, there probably wouldn’t be an issue if these segments alternated and were short – too short to affect the density surface model.  If the segments were long, then you might start to see an effect if you did relatively little smoothing in the DSM, especially at or near the edges of the study area.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Hi Scarlett,

It sounds like you have something odd going on with your updating algorithm. Are you sure you are calculating your acceptance probabilities correctly, proposing reasonable new values and storing the updated parameter values (as opposed to the current values)?

The detection function model should not be affected by whether you include absences or not as the data used here are the distances to the detections. Hence, the similarity between your first run and the results using the distance:ds() function.

The count model, on the other hand, will be affected by only using segments with detections (what you refer to as presences). I would think that if you combine all data you should have enough observations that will allow you to fit the model. So, please try your algorithm with all data first and see if you can get it to work.

I don't believe the problem lies in too many zeros, however. If your algorithm was reacting to the high number of zeros, your parameter values for the count model would update accordingly from your starting values, reflecting the low mean counts. I would recommend checking at each small step if the algorithm does the correct thing, i.e.
do the proposal distributions give a reasonable value?
is the acceptance probability calculated in the correct manner?
does the current parameter value get updated?
does the updated value get stored?
With regards to the proposal distributions, please remember that when using e.g. a normal distribution with a mean = current value and a fixed standard deviation, using small standard deviations will, on average, increase your chances of the newly proposed value being accepted and vice versa.

Hope this helps.

Cheers, Cornelia

At the moment, I am writing a discussion on population density estimation with the REM and CTDS for red deer and roe deer. While the results are very much comparable for one species, CTDS estimates are much lower with CTDS for the other.

Is this somehow considered in the CTDS estimates or could it potentially somehow be considered?

Maik

The proper way to organise your data so that the Distance package recognises you visited point count stations without making detections is shown in example data provided with the Distance package:

messages.body_plain:
Jesse

Good work on your part to have numerous transects and to be conscious of the challenges of conducting surveys from roads.  I'm not clear how your recording of habitat types for each detection will resolve the sampling from roads as it is unlikely that placement of roads will necessarily equitably sample the habitat types throughout the park, but that is another issue.

To your specific questions:

1 -  combine data from all five surveys into a single project.  You are unlikely to have much precision from analysing data from each night individually.

2 - not sure how to answer this.  The software fits a detection function to the perpendicular distances, then plots the fitted function superimposed upon the histogram of perpendicular distances.

3 - from your description of your design, I gather that you did not design your survey to explicitly lay transects into particular habitat types.  Consequently, the amount of survey effort in your habitat types will arise as a result of luck rather than as a result of design.  Perhaps you will have lots of detections in each of your habitats, but chances are that some of your habitats will have little effort (consequently few detections), making the assessment of detectability and encounter rate in those habitats challenging.  Nevertheless, the answer to your question is to create a field in the observation layer for habitat, because habitat type is associated with the detections, not with the transects, then conduct post-stratification.  Your GIS work of breaking a transect into bits will actually make it appear as if you have many more than the 32 transects you actually have, creating problems for estimating variability in encounter rates between transects.

4 - true, transect lengths are needed to estimate encounter rates, but transect lengths do not influence the detectability process governing the probability of detecting animals at various perpendicular distances from the transect.

If you want to discuss your issue #3 in more detail, we could have further correspondence off the list.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Eric et al.,

I am trying to understand some of the math in deriving the estimates based on surveys with cluster size variable. I have tried to dig into the source code of Distance/mrds, but cannot produce equivalent outputs. Any pointer and help hugely appreciated. I have to apologise in advance for any basic math mistakes I must have made...

Using the mink ClusterExercise from Distance as a reproducible example.

library(Distance)
library(tidyverse)
options(digits = 7)
data(ClusterExercise)
mod.cs <- ds(ClusterExercise)

Question 1: How is the Expected.S derived?

In the link below your response indicates that this is derived from the average observed group size in the sample.
https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/2W7DJtaB82Q/m/eg3f1BzNBAAJ

However, although that seems to be the case of the strata specific estimates, it does not seem to be the case for the total mean - as given in the output in ds.summary().

CALCULATED.Expected.cluster.size <- ClusterExercise %>%
  group_by(Region.Label) %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(size, na.rm=T)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  pull(mean)

DS.Expected.cluster.size <- summary(mod.cs)[["dht"]][["Expected.S"]][["Expected.S"]][-3]
all.equal(CALCULATED.Expected.cluster.size, DS.Expected.cluster.size) # TRUE

Calculating the overall survey wide mean cluster size

CALCULATED.TOTAL.Expected.cluster.size.total <- ClusterExercise %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(size, na.rm=T)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  pull(mean)

DS.TOTAL.Expected.cluster.size <- summary(mod.cs)[["dht"]][["Expected.S"]][["Expected.S"]][3]
all.equal(CALCULATED.TOTAL.Expected.cluster.size.total, DS.TOTAL.Expected.cluster.size) # FALSE

Not equivalent, and there is a difference of 0.05 in mean. Guess this is a relatively small number, but as it is also happening in my actual analysis I would like to know if there is some weighting of means going on?

Question 2: Getting the SE and CV for the Expected.S

Following the above attempt to derive Expected.S I have tried to estimate its SE and CV, which do not add up to what Distance provides me, based on the following steps, and referencing the following link:
  https://groups.google.com/g/distance-sampling/c/QYQ4Oysf9JY/m/aEkV6_JpAwAJ

# using outputs from ds
size.vct <- mod.cs[["ddf"]][["data"]][["size"]]
n.clst <- length(size.vct)

var.s <- var(size.vct, na.rm=T)
se.s <- sqrt(var.s/n.clst)
cv.s <- se.s/mean(size.vct) # mean not equivilant to ds Expected.S as per Q1
cv.s

I get cv.s = 0.1013096 and ds outputs cv.s = 0.2072411

Question 3: Deriving final estimates

# pulling the results from the mod.cs, I get:
average.p <- summary(mod.cs)[["ds"]][["average.p"]]
Expected.S <- summary(mod.cs)[["dht"]][["Expected.S"]][["Expected.S"]][3] # mean group size
effort <- summary(mod.cs)[["dht"]][["clusters"]][["summary"]][["Effort"]][[3]] #total effort
truncation <- summary(mod.cs)[["ddf"]][["meta.data"]][["int.range"]][2]

# and estimating D.hat, based on clustered group size, I get outputs which are not equivalent to the ds outputs:
# Using D = n * f(0) * E(s) / 2L
D.hat <-  n.clst *(1/average.p)*Expected.S/((2*truncation)*effort)
summary(mod.cs)

I get D.hat = 0.06556279 and ds gets D.hat = 0.05723343, similar, but not equivalent.

cv.s <- 0.2072411
ds.D.hat <- 0.05723343

se.D <- ds.D.hat * sqrt(cv.er <http://cv.er>^2 + cv.pa <http://cv.pa>^2 + cv.s^2)
cv.D <- se.D / ds.D.hat

Don Carlos

Detailed question and supporting calculations regarding computations involving animals occurring in groups.  The fundamental challenge with your work is the choice of data set.  Indeed this data set does include animals (minke whales) that occur in groups, but with the added complication that the survey employed stratification.  Hence the computations include not only details involved in group size, but also details involved in stratified estimates.  I think it is the later that is the cause of the discrepancies you describe.

Sprinkled below are some modifications to your calculations along with some narrative and supporting documentation

library(Distance)
data(ClusterExercise)
mod.cs <- ds(ClusterExercise)
thesummary <- summary(mod.cs)

Expected.S <- thesummary[["dht"]][["Expected.S"]][["Expected.S"]][3] # mean group size
effort <- thesummary[["dht"]][["clusters"]][["summary"]][["Effort"]] #effort
abundance.indiv <- thesummary[["dht"]][["individuals"]][["N"]][["Estimate"]] #abund indiv
abundance.groups <- thesummary[["dht"]][["clusters"]][["N"]][["Estimate"]] #abund group

Question 1 (expected group size)

For the study area, expected group size is the ratio of estimated individual abundance to estimated group abundance:

expected.group.size.studyarea <- abundance.indiv / abundance.groups
print(expected.group.size.studyarea)
print(thesummary$dht$Expected.S)

Question 2 (precision of estimated expected group size)

>From comments in the function dht.se <http://dht.se> in the mrds package:
>
> This computes the se(E(s)). It essentially uses 3.37 from Buckland et al. (2004) but in place of using 3.25, 3.34 and 3.38, it uses 3.27, 3.35 and an equivalent cov replacement term for 3.38. This uses line to line variability whereas the other formula measure the variance of E(s) within the lines and it goes to zero as p approaches 1.

Here is Eqn. 3.37

Question 3 (density in study area)

Because the study area was stratified, the overall density is a weighted mean of stratum-specific densities, with the weighting factor being the sizes of the respective strata.  See Buckland et al. (2001) Sect 3.7.1, Eqn 3.122 or equivalently (below) Buckland et al. (1993), Sect 3.8.1

area <- thesummary[["dht"]][["clusters"]][["summary"]][["Area"]] #area
density <- thesummary[["dht"]][["individuals"]][["D"]][["Estimate"]] #density

density.studyarea <- (area[1]/area[3] * density[1]) + (area[2]/area[3] * density[2])
print(density.studyarea)
print(density[3])

Question 3b (precision of overall density estimate)

Variance (or other measures of precision) of the density estimate from a stratified survey is described in Section 3.7.1 of Buckland et al. (2001) detailed in Eqns. 3.123 through 3.126; equivalently Buckland et al. (1993), Sect. 3.8.1 (below)

library(Distance)

          order=0, truncation=3, formula=~as.factor(Cue.type))

Hi Jamie,

Moving from t of 1 to 1.9 reduces temporal effort by almost half, so would almost double the abundance estimates for the same number of observations. If you also added more observations, abundance estimates will increase proportionally. If we double t and the n, the abundance estimate will quadruple (assuming the new observations don't cause a big change in the detection function). Changes in t and n will have bigger effects on the abundance estimate than small changes in the distribution of observed distances.

We expect upward bias in distances observed upon initial detection, e.g. if only the first image of each animal was included in the data. This is because animals approaching the camera from in front will be detected at the maximum sensor range, and not again, even if it proceeds towards the camera, where detection probability is supposed to be high (is assumed to be higher than at longer distances [monotonically increasing]). If cameras can be triggered again after recording an image, and we include those subsequent observations in our data, and the camera performs well enough to ensure that t is short enough that we get multiple observations of distance to some of the the same animals(s) as they move through the zone of potential detection, we're not as concerned about snapshot moments being predetermined. Observations of distance should be unbiased if (1) snapshot moments are predetermined, in which case we can chose any value for t without causing bias, or (2) t is small relative to how long it takes animals to travel through the zone of potential detection, such that the data describe animals' locations as they move through the sector, not only upon initial detection.

Could you explain what the table of results shows? I assume the values are estimated densities but I don't understand the column headings.

Eric
